title: At the market
goal: Shop for groceries, give quantities and weights, and understand how Arabic forms irregular plurals.
bekal: recognize the two kinds of plural and know when each is used
haggle politely and close a deal

dialogs.title: حِوَار — عِنْدَ بَائِعِ الْخُضَارِ
dialogs.intro: The morning market. Laila takes Budi shopping for cooking ingredients.

lines.speaker: لَيْلَى:
lines.text: صَبَاحَ الْخَيْرِ يَا عَمّ! كَيْفَ الْحَالُ؟
lines.id: Good morning, sir! How are things?
lines.literal: morning the-goodness O uncle! how the-condition?

lines.speaker: اَلْبَائِع:
lines.text: صَبَاحَ النُّورِ يَا بِنْتِي. تَفَضَّلِي، كُلُّ شَيْءٍ طَازَجٌ.
lines.baca: ṣabaahan-nuuri yaa bintii. tafaḍḍalii, kullu shai'in ṭaazaj.
lines.id: Good morning, dear. Go ahead, everything's fresh.
lines.literal: morning the-light O daughter-my. please, every thing fresh.

lines.speaker: لَيْلَى:
lines.text: أُرِيدُ كِيلُو طَمَاطِمَ وَنِصْفَ كِيلُو بَصَلٍ.
lines.baca: uriidu kiiluu ṭamaaṭima wa niṣfa kiiluu baṣal.
lines.id: I'd like a kilo of tomatoes and half a kilo of onions.
lines.literal: I-want kilo tomatoes and half kilo onions.

lines.speaker: اَلْبَائِع:
lines.id: Certainly. And fruit? I've got apples and bananas.
lines.literal: present. and the-fruit? at-me apples and bananas.

lines.speaker: بُودِي:
lines.id: How much is a kilo of apples?

lines.speaker: اَلْبَائِع:
lines.id: Twenty pounds. The bananas are fifteen.
lines.literal: for twenty pound. and the-bananas for fifteen.

lines.speaker: لَيْلَى:
lines.text: غَالٍ يَا عَمّ! أَمْسِ كَانَ بِثَمَانِيَةَ عَشَرَ.
lines.id: That's expensive, sir! Yesterday it was eighteen.
lines.literal: expensive O uncle! yesterday was for eighteen.

lines.speaker: اَلْبَائِع:
lines.text: خُذِي بِثَمَانِيَةَ عَشَرَ، لِأَنَّكِ زَبُونَةٌ قَدِيمَةٌ.
lines.id: Take them for eighteen, since you're a regular customer.
lines.literal: take(f) for eighteen, because-you(f) customer old.

lines.speaker: لَيْلَى:
lines.id: Thank you! And how much is it all together?

lines.speaker: بُودِي:
lines.id: Here you are. Do you have bags?

lines.speaker: اَلْبَائِع:
lines.id: Of course. Thank you, see you!

notes: **يَا عَمّ and يَا بِنْتِي don't mean actual family.** "Uncle" and "my daughter" are used with strangers as a polite, warm form of address — much like "sir", "ma'am" or "dear" in English. For someone your own age: يَا أَخِي (my brother), يَا أُخْتِي (my sister).

**صَبَاحَ الْخَيْرِ — why a fatha, not a damma?** The full form is a wish: "(may you have) a morning of goodness". Because it is the object of a dropped verb, it ends in a fatha. You don't need to understand the whole reason — just learn the sound as a whole.

**كُلُّ شَيْءٍ — "every thing" = everything.** كُلّ is always followed by a noun with a kasra: كُلُّ يَوْمٍ (every day), كُلُّ النَّاسِ (all the people). When a pronoun is attached to it, it means "all of it": اَلْمَجْمُوعُ كُلُّهُ ("the total, all of it").

**كِيلُو طَمَاطِمَ — idafa again.** "A kilo of tomatoes". The first word is bare, the second takes a kasra — but طَمَاطِم is one of the words that refuse tanween, so its kasra becomes a fatha: طَمَاطِمَ. Just recognize the phenomenon; don't memorize the list at this level.

**كَانَ — "was".** The past-tense verb that fills the gap left by the missing "is": أَمْسِ كَانَ بِثَمَانِيَةَ عَشَرَ ("yesterday it was eighteen"). كَانَ gets fully unpacked in unit 13; for now, just recognize that it marks the past.

**لِأَنَّ — "because".** It is always followed by a noun or an attached pronoun: لِأَنَّكِ (because you), لِأَنَّهُ (because he), لِأَنَّ الطَّعَامَ لَذِيذٌ (because the food is delicious). Same pattern as إِنَّ and لٰكِنَّ.
**خُذِي — a command to a woman.** From أَخَذَ (take): خُذْ (to a man), خُذِي (to a woman), خُذُوا (to several people). Adding ـِي for a woman works for every command form.
**بِالتَّمَامِ — "exactly", no change needed.** An everyday market expression confirming that the figure is a round one. Equivalent: بِالضَّبْطِ ("precisely").
**طَبْعًا — "of course".** One of the most frequently heard words in Arabic conversation. Equivalents: بِالتَّأْكِيدِ ("certainly"), أَكِيد ("for sure", more casual).

grammars.title: Two kinds of plural
body: Arabic forms plurals in two completely different ways, and unfortunately the irregular one is the one used most.
after: The sound plural is used mainly for **people** (and some feminine words). For things, it's almost always a broken plural — which has to be learned together with its singular, just like the middle vowel of verbs.
Once again: **learn them in pairs.** كِتَاب — كُتُب. Learning only the singular just postpones half the work until later, when you've forgotten the context.

grammars.title: Non-human plurals are treated as feminine singular
body: This is the rule that surprises learners most, and also the one broken most often. When the plural refers to **things**, its adjectives and verbs take the **feminine singular** form.
after: The dividing line is clear: **humans** get a real plural, **things and animals** are treated as one feminine thing. If in doubt, ask yourself: can this plural talk or not?

sections.title: At the market: groceries and units

blocks.text: Notice that the fruit and vegetable names above are **collective**: تُفَّاح means "apples" as a kind, not one apple. For a single one, add ة: تُفَّاحَة (an apple), مَوْزَة (a banana), بَيْضَة (an egg). This is the reverse of the usual rule — here ة makes the word singular.

blocks.title: Arabic plurals you may already know
items: A few Arabic words have entered English in their **plural form**, and English often treats them as ordinary nouns: *ulama* (عُلَمَاء, plural of عَالِم, "scholar"), *mujahideen* (plural of مُجَاهِد), *fellahin* (plural of فَلَّاح, "farmer"). Even *Bedouin* comes from a plural: بَدَوِيِّين, "desert dwellers".
This isn't just trivia: recognizing them gives you a few free Arabic words and shows you plural patterns through words you may already have met.

blocks.text: One thing textbooks rarely mention: **haggling is a conversation, not a fight.** The tone is light, sometimes joking, and it ends with both sides satisfied. If you haggle with a tense face, the seller will feel distrusted — and the price won't come down.

blocks.title: A lifesaver when sellers keep offering
items: If a seller keeps offering things you don't want, a polite but firm line: شُكْرًا، أَنَا أَتَفَرَّجُ فَقَطْ (*shukran, anaa atafarraju faqaṭ* — "thanks, I'm just looking").
And if you really want to move on: شُكْرًا، سَأَعُودُ لَاحِقًا ("thanks, I'll come back later"). Both are accepted without offense.

exercises.prompt: Choose the correct form of the adjective.

items: I'd like a kilo of tomatoes.
How much is a kilo of apples?
How much is it all together?

exercises.prompt: Build a market conversation: you want to buy two kilos of oranges and half a kilo of onions, ask the price, haggle, and agree.

answers: كُتُب — بُيُوت — أَقْلَام — طَالِبَات — مُهَنْدِسُونَ — أَوْلَاد
أُرِيدُ كِيلُو طَمَاطِمَ. — بِكَمْ كِيلُو التُّفَّاحِ؟ — هٰذَا غَالٍ جِدًّا. — كُلُّ شَيْءٍ طَازَجٌ. — كَمِ الْمَجْمُوعُ كُلُّهُ؟ — هَلْ عِنْدَكَ أَكْيَاسٌ؟

Example: صَبَاحَ الْخَيْرِ يَا عَمّ! — بِكَمْ كِيلُو الْبُرْتُقَالِ؟ — أُرِيدُ كِيلُوَيْنِ بُرْتُقَالًا وَنِصْفَ كِيلُو بَصَلٍ. — هٰذَا غَالٍ، آخِرُ سِعْرٍ؟ — خُذْ بِأَرْبَعِينَ جُنَيْهًا. — اِتَّفَقْنَا، شُكْرًا!
